newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy government and opposition clash over budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy government and opposition clash over budget.

text.p: Dialogue between Italy's centre-left government and the centre-right opposition over the draft 1997 budget appeared to have broken down on Monday as the lower house of parliament resumed examination of the package.

"Budget, the day of the break-up," declared the daily Corriere della Sera newspaper in a headline observing what it saw as increasingly tough stances adopted by the government and opposition over the stringent economic package.
Some half a million people demonstrated in Rome on Saturday against proposed tax hikes in the budget.
Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi on Sunday night accused the government of failing to listen to the people.
"The government has not realised the seriousness of our request," he said, referring to the opposition's demands to remove proxy measures in the budget.
The measures would give the government special powers to set policy on sensitive measures, including tax, without the need for parliamentary approval of the specific details.
The centre-left offered the opposition an olive branch on Sunday, saying it was willing to discuss details.
But media mogul Berlusconi rejected the move.
"We told the government that you cannot think about imposing taxes without discussing these taxes with parliament," Berlusconi told reporters on Sunday night.
"The government offered us a simple delay in the timing. It refused totally our request to discuss tax brackets, scales and items related to the payment of the tax."
Asked whether the dialogue had broken down, Berlusconi replied that the government had taken a decision.
"We note it with huge displeasure," he said.

Massimo D'Alema, leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) and the main party in government, said the march had "evidently gone to Berlusconi's head" and added that he did not know why the government's offer had been rejected.
"The government's offer should have been listened to. It would have reopened the parliamentary debate on fiscal matters. It has been rejected, and I don't know why."

The lower house has until November 14 to ratify the budget package, crucial to prime minister Romano Prodi's hopes of taking Italy into Europe's single currency, and which aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire from next year's projected deficit.
Commentators say Prodi may have to use confidence votes to sweep away expected opposition filibustering in the lower house. The government controls the Senate (upper house).
